title: Generic points and residue fields under finite scalar extension
statement: Let $F\subseteq K$ be a finite field extension and let $V$ be any $F$-scheme. Put $W=V\times_{\operatorname{Spec}F}\operatorname{Spec}K$ and let $\operatorname{pr}:W\to V$ be the projection. For every affine open $\operatorname{Spec}R\subseteq V$, its inverse image is $\operatorname{Spec}(R\otimes_F K)$; the corresponding map $R\to R\otimes_F K$ is finite free of rank $[K:F]$, and is flat. For every generic point $y$ of an irreducible component of $W$, the point $x=\operatorname{pr}(y)$ is a generic point of an irreducible component of $V$. For every point $y\in W$, with $x=\operatorname{pr}(y)$, its residue field $\kappa(y)$ is the quotient of the finite-dimensional $\kappa(x)$-algebra $\kappa(x)\otimes_F K$ by the prime corresponding to $y$ in the fibre over $x$; that quotient is a field, and $\kappa(y)/\kappa(x)$ is finite. Consequently, for any scheme $B$ and morphism $v:V\to B$ that sends every component generic point to a component generic point with finite residue extension, $v\circ\operatorname{pr}:W\to B$ has the same property. No normality or separability of $K/F$, finite-type or Noetherian hypothesis on $V$ or $B$, or reducedness is imposed. Fields and degree use [def-weil-field], [def-pc-field-extension], [def-pc-field-tower]; schemes, spectrum, fibre products, generic points, components, residue fields and flatness use [def-pc-scheme], [def-weil-affine-spectrum], [def-pc-fibre-product], [def-sc-generic-point], [def-weil-irreducible-components], [def-weil-residue-field], [def-weil-flat-morphism]. Tensor products, free modules and flat ring maps use [def-weil-pbc-module-tensor-product], [def-weil-pbc-free-module] and [def-weil-pbc-flat-ring-map].

proof.text: Fix an affine open $U=\operatorname{Spec}R\subseteq V$. Apply [lem-weil-pbc-open-fibre-product] to the opens $U\subseteq V$, the whole $\operatorname{Spec}K$, and the whole $\operatorname{Spec}F$. It identifies $\operatorname{pr}^{-1}(U)$ with $U\times_{\operatorname{Spec}F}\operatorname{Spec}K$, compatibly with its projection to $U$. By [lem-weil-pbc-fibre-product-affine-spectra] this is $\operatorname{Spec}S$, where $S=R\otimes_F K$, and its map to $U$ is induced by $r\mapsto r\otimes1$.

Put $n=[K:F]$ and choose an $F$-basis $b_1,\ldots,b_n$ of $K$, with coordinate functions $\lambda_i:K\to F$. The mutually inverse $R$-linear maps are $R^n\to S$, $(r_i)\mapsto\sum_i r_i\otimes b_i$, and $S\to R^n$, $r\otimes k\mapsto(r\lambda_i(k))_i$. The second is well-defined by the tensor-product relations, and the inverse identities follow from $k=\sum_i\lambda_i(k)b_i$ and $\lambda_i(b_j)=\delta_{ij}$. Thus $1\otimes b_i$ is an $R$-basis: $S$ is finite free of rank $n$. These formulas also hold for $R=0$.

source.place: Agent-written coordinate calculation from the tensor universal property of Tag 00CX (lemma-tensor-product); finite freeness means a finite basis (Tag 00C2, item-free-module).

proof.text: To check flatness directly, for any $R$-module $N$ the basis in step 2 identifies $N\otimes_R S$ with $N^n$: $a\otimes s\mapsto(c_i a)_i$ when $s=\sum_i c_i(1\otimes b_i)$, with inverse $(a_i)\mapsto\sum_i a_i\otimes(1\otimes b_i)$. For an injective map $f:N_1\to N_2$, $f\otimes1$ becomes $(a_i)\mapsto(f(a_i))$, which is injective coordinate by coordinate. This is precisely the definition of a flat ring map in [def-weil-pbc-flat-ring-map], proving the flatness of $R\to S$. The same coordinates preserve exactness: if $(a_i)$ maps to zero in the next module, choose a preimage of each $a_i$ in the preceding module; the resulting tuple is a preimage of $(a_i)$. Thus the calculation also satisfies the exact-sequence formulation in Stacks 00HB.

source.place: Tag 00HB (definition-flat), items (1) and (3); agent-written coordinate verification rather than an uncited free-implies-flat lemma.

proof.text: We spell out the passage between component generic points and an open neighbourhood. If $z\in O\subseteq X$ with $O$ open, then $C=\overline{\{z\}}$ has $C\cap O=\overline{\{z\}}^{\,O}$. If $C$ is maximal irreducible in $X$, an irreducible closed subset of $O$ containing $C\cap O$ has irreducible closure in $X$ containing $C$, hence equals $C$ after closure; intersecting with $O$ gives equality. Conversely, if $C\cap O$ is maximal irreducible in $O$, any irreducible closed $Z\supseteq C$ has nonempty open $Z\cap O$, hence dense in $Z$: two nonempty relative opens intersect by irreducibility. It follows that $Z\cap O=C\cap O$, and taking closures gives $Z=C$. Thus $z$ is a component generic point in $X$ if and only if it is one in $O$. For $O=\operatorname{Spec}A$, its closure is $V(\mathfrak q)$ when $z=\mathfrak q$: $V(\mathfrak q)$ is closed, and every closed $V(I)$ containing $\mathfrak q$ contains $V(\mathfrak q)$. Consequently [lem-weil-pbc-spec-irreducible-components-minimal-primes] identifies this condition with minimality of $\mathfrak q$.

source.place: Tag 00ES (lemma-irreducible), parts (1) and (3); open-neighbourhood argument written out from irreducibility and closure definitions.

proof.text: Now let $y$ be a component generic point of $W$, let $x=\operatorname{pr}(y)$, and choose the affine neighbourhood of $x$ in step 1. Write $\mathfrak q\subset S$ for $y$ and $\mathfrak p=\mathfrak q\cap R$ for $x$. Step 4 says that $\mathfrak q$ is minimal. If $\mathfrak p_0\subseteq\mathfrak p$ is any prime of $R$, flatness from step 3 and [lem-sc-flat-going-down] supply a prime $\mathfrak q_0\subseteq\mathfrak q$ contracting to $\mathfrak p_0$. Minimality gives $\mathfrak q_0=\mathfrak q$, so $\mathfrak p_0=\mathfrak p$. Thus $\mathfrak p$ is minimal. By step 4, $x$ is a component generic point first in $U$ and then in $V$. No existence or finiteness assertion about a list of components is used.

source.place: Tag 00HS (lemma-flat-going-down), applied to the finite-free map of steps 2–3.

proof.text: For any $y\in W$ put $x=\operatorname{pr}(y)$ and $D=\kappa(x)\otimes_F K$. By [lem-weil-pbc-fibre-product-points], $y$ corresponds to a prime $P$ of $D$; the other two residue fields are $K$ and $F$ because spectra of fields have their single points [def-weil-affine-spectrum]. By the fibre definition and the fibre-product universal property, a map $T\to W_x$ is a pair of maps $T\to\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(x)$ and $T\to\operatorname{Spec}K$ agreeing over $\operatorname{Spec}F$: the map to $V$ is forced by the first map. Hence $W_x=\operatorname{Spec}D$, compatibly with both projections, and this is the prime in the stated fibre. The basis calculation of step 2 with $R=\kappa(x)$ gives dimension $n$ for $D$; the images of its $n$ basis vectors span $D/P$. This quotient is a nonzero domain because $P$ is prime. Hence [lem-weil-pbc-finite-dimensional-domain-is-field] makes $D/P$ a field. Apply the final clause of [lem-weil-pbc-fibre-product-point-residue-field]: the canonical $D/P\to\kappa(y)$ is an isomorphism compatible with $\kappa(x)\to\kappa(y)$. This proves both the asserted quotient description and finiteness of $\kappa(y)/\kappa(x)$.

source.place: Tag 01JT (lemma-points-fibre-product), including its residue-field sentence; Tag 01I4 for the fibre spectrum. The finite-dimensional-domain ingredient is the existing Mathlib leaf.

proof.text: Finally take a component generic point $y$ of $W$. Step 5 makes $x=\operatorname{pr}(y)$ a component generic point of $V$, and the hypothesis on $v$ makes $b=v(x)$ a component generic point of $B$. The induced residue maps compose: on local rings the stalk map for a composite is the composite stalk map, and passing to maximal-ideal quotients gives $\kappa(b)\to\kappa(x)\to\kappa(y)$, the residue map for $v\circ\operatorname{pr}$ [def-weil-residue-field]. Both extensions are finite. Explicitly, products of members of a finite $\kappa(b)$-spanning set of $\kappa(x)$ with members of a finite $\kappa(x)$-spanning set of $\kappa(y)$ span $\kappa(y)$ over $\kappa(b)$. Thus the composite has the required finite residue extension. If $W$ is empty the generic-point assertions are vacuous; all preceding affine calculations remain valid.
